title: Permission to share other people's information

sections.skill: Decide whether you may share other people's information

questions.prompt: Before pasting a coworker's performance review into an AI tool, what should you ask?

choices.text: Will the tool write a better review than mine?
Do I have permission to share it with this tool?
Is the review long enough to paste?
Does the coworker use the same tool?

questions.correct_answer: Do I have permission to share it with this tool?
questions.intro: Information about other people is not yours to share freely. A customer's order details, a classmate's essay, a patient's chart or a coworker's performance review was given to you for a specific purpose. Before pasting it into an AI tool, ask: Do I have PERMISSION (from the person, or from my school or employer's rules) to share it with this tool? Many schools and workplaces have written rules about which AI tools may be used with which data, and some types of data, such as health or student records, have legal protections. When in doubt, ask before sharing.

sections.skill: Compare sharing information with lending a borrowed book

questions.prompt: Can you lend a borrowed book to a stranger without asking?

choices.text: Yes, if the stranger is nice
Yes, books belong to everyone
Probably not; it was lent to you
Only on weekends

questions.correct_answer: Probably not; it was lent to you
questions.intro: Your friend lends you a book. Can you lend it to a stranger? Probably not without asking: the book was lent to YOU for YOU to read. Information about others works the same way. A classmate who shares an essay for you to review, or a customer who gives an address for delivery, has lent you that information for one purpose. Passing it on, including pasting it into an AI tool, needs their permission or a rule that allows it.

questions.prompt: A classmate shared an essay for you to review. Is pasting it into a tool like lending the book?

questions.intro: Permission has limits. A customer who gave an address for delivery did not agree to have it used for anything else. An employer may approve one AI tool for confidential documents but not another. A friend who shares a story in confidence has not agreed to have it pasted anywhere. Permission can also be specific to purpose: summarizing a document internally may be allowed while uploading it to a public tool is not. When rules are unclear, ask the person or the responsible office, and keep a note of the answer.
